---
id: c-flood-depth
title: Recursion Depth vs Explicit Stack
difficulty: Hard
order: 2
tags: recursion, stack overflow, iterative DFS
---
## Statement
Count the connected regions of `.` cells in an `r × c` grid of `.` and `#` (4-directional), and print the size of the largest region.

The grid can be as large as **2000 × 2000**, and one region may be a single snake-like path through millions of cells. A recursive flood fill will **overflow the stack** (segmentation fault) on the large hidden test. Use an **explicit stack** allocated on the heap.

## Starter
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    int r, c;
    if (scanf("%d %d", &r, &c) != 2) return 1;

    return 0;
}
```


## Hints
- Read the grid into `char *g = malloc(r * c)`, reading each row with `scanf("%s", ...)` into a temporary buffer.
- `int *stack = malloc(sizeof(int) * r * c)` holds cell indices `i * c + j`. Mark a cell visited (e.g. set it to `#`) **when you push it**.
- Pop, count, and push the unvisited open neighbours.

## Solution
Each cell is pushed at most once (it's marked when pushed), so a heap-allocated stack of size r·c always suffices. The recursion depth problem disappears because there's no recursion.

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    int r, c;
    if (scanf("%d %d", &r, &c) != 2) return 1;
    char *g = malloc((size_t)r * c);
    char *row = malloc((size_t)c + 2);
    int *stack = malloc(sizeof(int) * (size_t)r * c);
    if (!g || !row || !stack) return 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < r; i++) {
        scanf("%s", row);
        for (int j = 0; j < c; j++) g[i * c + j] = row[j];
    }
    int regions = 0, best = 0;
    for (int start = 0; start < r * c; start++) {
        if (g[start] != '.') continue;
        regions++;
        int top = 0, size = 0;
        stack[top++] = start;
        g[start] = '#';
        while (top > 0) {
            int cur = stack[--top];
            size++;
            int i = cur / c, j = cur % c;
            int nb[4][2] = {{i + 1, j}, {i - 1, j}, {i, j + 1}, {i, j - 1}};
            for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
                int ni = nb[k][0], nj = nb[k][1];
                if (ni >= 0 && ni < r && nj >= 0 && nj < c && g[ni * c + nj] == '.') {
                    g[ni * c + nj] = '#';
                    stack[top++] = ni * c + nj;
                }
            }
        }
        if (size > best) best = size;
    }
    printf("%d %d\n", regions, best);
    free(stack);
    free(row);
    free(g);
    return 0;
}
```

A recursive version, `void fill(i, j) { ...; fill(i+1, j); ... }`, is shorter and works on small grids, but on the snake test its depth reaches about 2 million frames (well over 100 MB of stack against an 8 MB limit) and it crashes. Knowing when recursion depth is unbounded, and replacing it with an explicit stack, is a core systems-programming skill.
